reconcile.connective: Defenders deny any conflict by reading the conquest summaries as a promise of gradual, not immediate, dispossession — so the land could be "given" while Canaanites remained.

discrepancy.connective: Steve Wells sets the very texts side by side, arguing that the triumphal summaries — Joshua 21:43-44's claim that the Lord delivered every enemy and gave Israel all the land — cannot stand beside Joshua 15-17 and Judges 1's admission that the Jebusites and other Canaanites were never driven out.

skeptic.name: Steve Wells
skeptic.work: The Skeptic's Annotated Bible, "Did God destroy the nations?"
skeptic.attribution: Steve Wells, The Skeptic's Annotated Bible (2013), "Did God destroy the nations?" (skepticsannotatedbible.com/contra/driveout.html)

excerpts.excerpt_text: Notwithstanding the fact that many a tract of country still remained in the hands of the Canaanites, the promise that the land of Canaan should be given to the house of Israel for a possession had been fulfilled; for God had not promised the immediate and total destruction of the Canaanites, but only their gradual extermination (Exo 23:29-30; Deu 7:22).
excerpts.on_tension_rationale: Directly answers the core tension: it concedes Canaanites still remained yet argues Josh 21:43-45's 'all the land given' is not falsified, because the promise was gradual extermination, not immediate total conquest. Strongest, most self-contained harmonization on the row; distinct anchor-block voice (K&D).

pd_work.resource: Keil & Delitzsch, Biblical Commentary on the Old Testament, on Joshua 21:43-45 (1861-75)
pd_work.author: Keil & Delitzsch
pd_work.note: K&D treat this passage directly, harmonizing Josh 21:43-45's 'all the land' summary with the surviving Canaanites by appeal to the promised gradual (not immediate total) dispossession of Exo 23:29-30 and Deu 7:22, and quote Calvin to the same end. Used in place of Haley because Haley's coverage of this specific passage could not be confirmed.
